data.title: Nvidia falls 2.9% after record results; it has closed below its open after 9 of 10 reports
data.description:
Nvidia shares fell 2.9% on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, the first full session after the company reported record revenue and raised its growth target for next year. Before the market opened the stock had been up 2.9%. It closed at $150.96, its lowest close since June 2025, according to Nasdaq prices.

The slide fits a pattern, and one detail breaks it. TECHi went through Nvidia's last ten earnings reports. On nine of them the stock finished the next session below the price at which it opened, and on seven it ended lower than it had closed before the results. This time its closest rivals did not fall with it. AMD rose 5.3% and Broadcom 3.6%.

What happened to Nvidia stock on Wednesday?

The results came out after the close on Tuesday. Revenue was $115.84 billion, above the top of Nvidia's own forecast range, and the company guided to $130 billion for the current quarter. The shares rose about 4% in after-hours trading.

They held most of that overnight. Nasdaq's minute-by-minute pre-market data peaks at $161.66 at 5:06 a.m. Eastern, 4.0% above Tuesday's close of $155.46. At 6:39 a.m. the price was $159.89, as TECHi reported this morning.

The gain did not survive the opening bell. Nvidia began regular trading at about $158.94, up 2.2%, and that was close to the best price of the day. The session high was $159.70. By 9:42 a.m. the stock was below Tuesday's close. It fell as low as $150.40 and finished at $150.96. About 339 million shares changed hands.

In market value the move is large. On Nvidia's 24.2 billion diluted shares, the 6:39 a.m. price was worth about $107 billion more than Tuesday's close. The closing price is worth about $109 billion less. The difference between the two, roughly $216 billion, went in under ten hours.

Nvidia has now fallen in seven of the eight sessions since November 6 and is down 19.1% over that stretch. Tuesday's close had already been its lowest in a year. Wednesday's is lower still.

How often does Nvidia fall after earnings?

More often than it rises. Nvidia publishes its results after the market closes, so the next session is the first in which every investor can trade on them. TECHi took the dates of Nvidia's last ten results releases from its SEC filings and compared three Nasdaq prices for each: the close before the results, the next day's open and the next day's close.

On seven of the ten, the stock closed lower the next day than it had before the results. The average move across all ten is a fall of 1.6%.

The pattern inside the day is stronger. On nine of the ten, Nvidia closed below its opening price. Buyers who waited for the open on the morning after paid more than the stock was worth by the close on every occasion but one.

A strong open has not been protection. Nvidia opened at least 2% higher on six of the ten mornings, including Wednesday. On five of those six it closed below its open. The largest reversal was on February 27, 2025, when the stock opened 2.8% higher and closed 8.5% lower. On November 20, 2025 it opened 5.1% higher and closed 3.2% lower.

The exception is the report before this one. On August 27, 2026 the stock opened 6.3% higher and added to the gain, closing up 8.7%.

Across the ten sessions the average move from open to close is a fall of 3.5%. Wednesday's, at 5.0%, is the third-largest of the ten.

Why did AMD and Broadcom rise?

The prices suggest investors are treating Nvidia's problems as Nvidia's own. AMD closed at $530.14, up 5.3%. Broadcom closed at $354.05, up 3.6%. Both sell chips for AI data centers, and Nvidia's results were good news for that market. Its data center revenue rose 110% from a year earlier.

On earlier day-after sessions the stocks tended to move together. AMD fell on four of the six previous days when Nvidia fell, and when it rose it rose less than 1%. Wednesday's gap of 8.2 points in AMD's favour is the widest of the ten.

The rest of the group split. Before the open, the ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracked this morning were up 4.0% on average. By the close the average gain was 0.7%, and six of the ten finished higher. AMD, Arista Networks and Broadcom gained the most, at 5.3%, 4.0% and 3.6%. CoreWeave, Dell and Marvell lost the most, at 4.1%, 2.9% and 2.2%.

Two of those three depend directly on Nvidia's products. CoreWeave rents out computing capacity that runs on Nvidia chips, and Dell builds them into servers. The stocks that rose most sell alternatives or the networks that connect them.

The four largest spenders on AI data centers did better than they had before the open. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta were up 0.6% on average in pre-market trading. They ended up 1.2% on average, and Amazon did best with a gain of 3.8%. The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4%.

Since November 6 Nvidia is down 19.1% and AMD is up 18.1%, a gap of 37.2 percentage points. It was 28.8 points at Tuesday's close.

Is the fall about the results?

The numbers Nvidia reported give little reason for it. Revenue beat the top of the forecast range by $5.7 billion. The adjusted gross margin of 74.9% was above the top of its range as well. Interim chief executive Colette Kress raised the company's growth target for next fiscal year to 75% from 70%, as TECHi reported on Tuesday.

There are softer points. The $130 billion outlook covers a 14-week quarter, and per week it implies growth of about 4%, TECHi's analysis of the results showed. Nvidia also forecast a gross margin between 71% and 72%, down from 74.8%.

What the results could not settle is who will run the company. Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive was announced on November 12. The board has said it does not intend to reinstate him and has hired a search firm to find a successor. Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing a person familiar with the matter, that the firm has contacted Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm, and has begun approaching other executives. An approach is not an appointment. The board has given no date for one and no update on its investigation.

The valuation gap is wide. At $150.96, Nvidia trades at 9.7 times the earnings analysts expect for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028, on Nasdaq's consensus of $15.55 a share. AMD, at $530.14, trades at 33.1 times its expected 2027 earnings.

The record has limits. Ten reports is a small sample, and each one landed in a different market. Three of the earlier declines came on days when AMD and Broadcom each fell more than 2% as well. Wednesday was not one of those days.

Nor has the pattern reversed quickly. About a month after seven of the nine earlier reports, Nvidia was still below its pre-results close. The two exceptions, in May 2025 and August 2026, followed the two largest day-after gains. That is a record of what happened, and it does not say what will happen this time.

What to watch

The Commerce Department's chip export rule is scheduled to take effect on Thursday, and China has said it will respond. For Nvidia itself the dates are a quarterly report due by December 4 and the naming of a permanent chief executive, which has no date. AMD reports its December quarter in early February. If the discount on Nvidia is about leadership, the next sharp move in the gap is more likely to follow an appointment than a set of numbers. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and AMD carry live prices.

data.title: Coherent sets $2 billion buyback, the same sum Nvidia paid for its stake in March
data.description:
Coherent Corp.'s board has authorized the company to buy back up to $2.0 billion of its own stock, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The program has no end date and does not oblige the company to buy a single share. Coherent's stock was up 10.1% at $234.27 at 9:56 a.m. Eastern, about twice the gain of other makers of optical parts for AI data centers.

The figure has a counterpart. In March, Nvidia paid $2.0 billion for 7.79 million new Coherent shares at $256.80 each. Coherent closed at $212.84 on Wednesday, 17% below that price. At Wednesday's close the same $2.0 billion would buy 9.40 million shares, 1.6 million more than the company issued to Nvidia, TECHi's calculation shows. There is a complication. Coherent's operations and capital spending together used $868 million of cash in its latest quarter, and the company holds less unrestricted cash than the full program would cost.

What did Coherent announce?

The filing is three paragraphs long. It says the board authorized the program on Wednesday, November 18, and that the company may repurchase up to $2.0 billion of its common stock, not counting fees and commissions.

It gives the company a wide choice of methods. Purchases can be made in the open market, in negotiated deals including accelerated buybacks, in block trades through a broker, under pre-arranged trading plans, or by selling put options and using other derivatives.

It also sets out how little is promised. The program has no expiration date. It does not oblige Coherent to buy any particular number of shares, and it may be suspended or stopped at any time.

The filing does not say why the board acted now, how purchases will be paid for or when they will begin. It is signed by the chief financial officer, Sherri Luther, and has no press release attached.

Coherent makes lasers and optical components. Most of its revenue now comes from its data center and communications business, which includes the optical parts that move data between servers in AI data centers. The quarterly report it filed on November 4 makes no mention of a repurchase program. The only shares the company took in last quarter were about 435,000 withheld from employees to cover tax on stock awards, at a cost of $128.6 million.

How much stock would $2 billion buy?

That depends on the price, and the price has moved a long way this year.

At Wednesday's close of $212.84, $2.0 billion buys 9.40 million shares. Coherent had 196.96 million shares outstanding on November 2, so that is 4.8% of the company.

The same sum would have bought far less in June. Coherent's highest close of the past year was $426.89 on June 2. By Wednesday the stock had halved. At the June price, $2.0 billion covered 4.69 million shares, or 2.4%.

The low since that peak came this month. Coherent fell 13% on November 5, the day after it reported quarterly results, to close at $169.76. It had recovered 25% from there by Wednesday.

A buyback would also offset some recent dilution. Coherent had about 155.6 million shares outstanding at the end of June 2025 and 196.9 million at the end of September 2026, an increase of 27%. Most of that came from 30.1 million shares issued when preferred stock was converted late last year and from the shares sold to Nvidia. The full program, spent at Wednesday's price, would reverse a little under a quarter of the increase.

Why does the Nvidia sale matter?

Because it was the same amount of money going the other way, at a higher price.

On March 2, Coherent sold 7,788,161 new shares to Nvidia at $256.80 each, for $2.0 billion in cash. The sale came with a multi-year supply agreement, including what the companies called a multi-billion-dollar purchase commitment from Nvidia. Coherent said the money would support research, new capacity and its operations as it expands manufacturing in the United States. Its shares rose 15% that day.

Nvidia still held every one of those shares on September 30, according to its latest holdings report, which valued them at $2.24 billion. A six-month restriction on selling them has ended. The purchase agreement also contained what Coherent calls a price protection provision, which ran for six months. The quarterly report says it expired in September without being triggered.

Since then the price has dropped below what Nvidia paid. Coherent last closed above $256.80 on October 14. At Wednesday's close the stake was worth $1.66 billion, $342 million less than it cost.

That gap is the arithmetic in favor of the board's decision. Coherent issued 7.79 million shares for $2.0 billion. If it spent $2.0 billion at Wednesday's price it would retire 9.40 million. The company would have taken in and paid out the same sum and ended, all else equal, with 1.6 million fewer shares than it had before the Nvidia deal.

Two cautions apply. The filing does not connect the program to Nvidia's money, and that money was raised to pay for expansion. And the sum only works below $256.80. Thursday's rise moved the stock closer to that level.

Can Coherent afford it?

Not from the cash it held at the end of September, if it also keeps building at the present rate.

Business is strong. Revenue in the three months to September 30 was $2.37 billion, up 50% from a year earlier. Sales to data center and communications customers rose 79% to $1.95 billion and made up 82% of the total. Net earnings were $384.7 million, or $1.90 a share.

Cash moved the other way. Coherent's operations used $92.7 million in the quarter, and the largest single item was a $737 million increase in inventory. Capital spending was $775.5 million, more than seven times the $103.9 million of a year earlier. Together that is an outflow of $868 million.

The company covered it in two ways. Subsidiaries outside the United States borrowed $773 million under new local credit lines, and Coherent ran down its short-term investments by $625 million.

At the end of September it had $1.55 billion of cash and $200 million of short-term investments, or $1.75 billion in all. A further $583 million was restricted. Total debt was $4.00 billion, up from $3.22 billion three months earlier.

So the program is larger than the unrestricted cash Coherent held. It equals a little more than five quarters of net earnings at the latest rate. Unless cash flow turns, buying the full amount would mean borrowing more or buying slowly. The absence of an end date allows for the second.

Management expects the business to keep growing. On November 4 it forecast revenue of $2.55 billion to $2.75 billion for the current quarter and said it expects its first $3 billion quarter by the end of its fiscal year next June.

How did the stock react?

Coherent was at $234.27 at 9:56 a.m. Eastern on Thursday, up 10.1% from Wednesday's close, according to Nasdaq's minute-by-minute data. That adds about $4.2 billion to the company's market value, 2.1 times the size of the program.

Not all of that is the buyback. AI hardware stocks rose broadly on Thursday morning, as TECHi reported before the open. Lumentum, Coherent's closest listed rival in optical components, was up 5.1% at about the same time. Ciena was up 5.5% and Nvidia 2.9%. Coherent's gain was roughly 5 points more than the two optical companies'.

The move takes the stock back to about where it stood a week ago. It closed at $234.51 on November 11 and was 13% lower by November 16, a stretch in which AI stocks fell after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive, as TECHi reported.

At Thursday morning's price the arithmetic above is a little weaker. $2.0 billion buys 8.54 million shares at $234.27, 0.7 million more than Nvidia received. Nvidia's stake is worth $1.82 billion, $175 million below its cost.

There is a case on each side. The stock is still 45% below its June high after Thursday's rise while revenue has grown by half, the share count is a quarter higher than in mid-2025, and the board is signalling that it sees value at this price. Against that, an authorization is not a purchase. The company is spending more than it earns on factories and inventory, its debt rose by $778 million in a single quarter, and money spent on shares is not available for expansion.

One further fact bears on how the program will be judged. In August the board's compensation committee granted special stock awards to senior executives, among them one with a target value of $50 million for chief executive Jim Anderson. They vest only if the share price reaches set milestones and other conditions are met through 2030, a company filing shows.

What to watch

Coherent's next quarterly report, due around early February, has to show how many shares it bought and at what average price. Free cash flow for the December quarter will show whether the outflow is narrowing. Nvidia's next holdings report, in mid-February, will show whether it still owns its 7.79 million shares. The method matters too: an accelerated buyback retires a large block at once, while open-market buying can take years. TECHi's Coherent quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Anthropic ends first day at $97.17, up 17%; half its opening jump was gone by the close
data.description:
Anthropic closed its first day of trading at $97.17 on Thursday, November 19, 2026, 17.1% above the $83 price of its initial public offering, Nasdaq data show. The shares opened at $111.50, touched $115.10 and were below $100 within 17 minutes of the first trade. About 857 million changed hands.

TECHi's calculations put numbers on the day. The opening price was a gain of $28.50 a share on the offer price, and the close kept $14.17 of it, almost exactly half. On the 13.22 billion shares in Anthropic's final prospectus, the company ended the day worth $1.28 trillion. That is $187 billion more than at the offer price and $189 billion less than at its first trade. The stock slipped again after the close, to $92.58. It was at $90.94 in pre-market trading at 5:16 a.m. on Friday.

How did the first day go?

Trading began late in the morning, as it usually does for a large new listing while the exchange matches opening orders. Nasdaq's minute-by-minute data show the first prices at 11:48 a.m. Eastern.

The official opening price was $111.50, 34.3% above the offer. The day's high, reached before noon, was $115.10, or 38.7% above it. The strength did not last. By 12:05 p.m. the stock was under $100. At about 1:18 p.m. it reached its low of $92.72, which was still 11.7% above the offer price.

It spent the afternoon between about $93 and $98 and closed at $97.17. Of the 252 one-minute readings in the regular session, 214 were below $100. After 11:54 a.m. none was at or above the opening price.

The shares kept falling once the market closed. The lowest late reading was $91.63 at 7:38 p.m., and the last, at 7:59 p.m., was $92.58. That is 4.7% below the close and 11.5% above the offer price.

Pre-market trading on Friday pointed the same way. At 5:16 a.m. Eastern the stock was at $90.94, 6.4% below Thursday's close and 9.6% above the offer price. On the prospectus share count that is about $1.20 trillion. Trading at those hours is thin and Friday's opening price may differ.

What is Anthropic worth after one day?

The final prospectus counts 13,219,642,276 shares of all classes after the offering and the private sale that ran beside it, before any shares the underwriters may add. At $97.17 that is $1.28 trillion. At the $83 offer price it was $1.10 trillion, and at the opening price it was $1.47 trillion.

Larger figures are in circulation because they count more shares. Adding stock options, unvested awards and notes that have yet to convert, TECHi's tally is about 17.6 billion shares, as in its report on the pricing. On that count the company was worth about $1.71 trillion at the close. Investing.com put the figure at about $1.76 trillion.

The price asks more of the business than it did on Wednesday. Anthropic's revenue was $17.0 billion in the third quarter. At the closing value, investors are paying 18.9 times that quarter's revenue multiplied by four. At the offer price it was 16.1 times. The company reported an operating loss of $1.26 billion for the first nine months of the year.

Who gained on day one?

Buyers in the offering did. The 980 million shares sold at $83 were worth $14.17 more each by the close, a combined gain of $13.9 billion.

The company's side of that is the usual cost of a first-day rise. Anthropic sold 956.4 million of those shares. At the closing price they would have brought in $13.6 billion more. Measured against the opening price the gap was $27.3 billion.

The seven co-founders sold 3,378,378 shares each in the offering, $1.96 billion between them. The prospectus shows them holding 1.67 billion shares afterward. Those were worth $162.6 billion at the close, about $23 billion apiece.

Amazon and Google hold the largest stakes the prospectus spells out. It says Amazon will hold 1,936,452,353 shares after the offering, 14.6% of the company, and Google 1,774,959,745, or 13.4%. At the close those stakes come to $188.2 billion and $172.5 billion. That is $27.4 billion and $25.2 billion more than at the offer price. Their shares are a non-voting class that does not trade, so these are values at the listed share price and not prices anyone was paid. Amazon also holds notes that have not converted because of an ownership cap.

The seven companies that bought $26.0 billion of stock in the private sale ended the day $4.4 billion ahead on paper. Nvidia's 120.5 million shares, bought for about $10.0 billion, were worth $11.7 billion. AMD's $2.5 billion had become $2.93 billion. Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft, at about $1.0 billion each, held stock worth $1.17 billion, and TSMC's $500 million was worth $585 million. That stock is restricted and cannot be resold freely at once.

Who is sitting on a loss?

Anyone who bought at the open. A buyer at $111.50 was down 12.9% by the close and 17.0% at the last late reading. A buyer at the day's high was down 15.6% by the close.

Trading was heavy. Volume was 857.3 million shares, equal to 87% of the 980 million sold in the offering and 6.5% of all shares outstanding. At the closing price that is $83.3 billion of stock in one session, more than the $81.3 billion the offering itself raised.

The offer price itself was never tested. The lowest reading in Nasdaq's data for Thursday, $91.63 in late trading, was 10.4% above it.

The data do not show who sold. Investors allotted stock at $83 could sell at a profit all day. Up to 316 million shares held by employees and other insiders were also free to be sold from the first day, as TECHi's release calendar showed. At the close those were worth $30.7 billion.

Did the debut help other AI stocks?

Not by the close. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25% to 23,879.20, which Investing.com said was a seven-month low. Nvidia lost 3.3% to end at $145.98 and AMD lost 7.7%. Microsoft fell 2.0%.

Those two holders fell too. Amazon lost 3.9% and Alphabet 3.5% on the day their stakes gained $27.4 billion and $25.2 billion on paper.

The morning had looked different. Ten AI hardware stocks were up 3.9% on average before the open, as TECHi reported, and Nvidia was up 2.1%. TECHi has not established why the market turned, and the timing alone does not show that the listing caused it.

What comes next?

The offering is due to close on Friday, when the prospectus says the shares will be delivered. The underwriters hold an option to buy 147 million more shares from the company at the offer price, worth $12.2 billion. With the stock above $83 they have a reason to use it.

The supply of shares grows from here. The first timed release under the lock-up agreements falls on December 15. By February 2, up to 1.61 billion shares can become eligible for sale. At Thursday's close that is $156.6 billion of stock, 1.9 times the volume of the first day.

What to watch

Friday's opening price, set against Thursday's close of $97.17 and the pre-market reading of $90.94. Whether the stock holds above the $83 offer price, which is where the underwriters' option and the private buyers' cost sit. Any filing on the option. Anthropic's first results as a public company, which also set the dates of the largest early share releases. TECHi's quote pages for Amazon, Alphabet and Nvidia carry live prices.

data.title: Everpure revenue jumps 51%, $125M above its forecast; inventory is up fivefold this year
data.description:
Everpure, the data storage company formerly called Pure Storage, reported revenue of $1.46 billion for the three months to November 1, 2026, up 51% from a year earlier, according to results released after the market closed on Wednesday, November 18. That is $125 million above the top of the range the company gave in August. It raised its full-year forecast for the third quarter in a row.

Two details sit behind the headline. Most of the raise is revenue already earned: $130 million of the $155 million added to the full-year midpoint is the amount by which the latest quarter beat its forecast, TECHi's calculation shows. And the growth is absorbing cash. Inventory has grown fivefold since the fiscal year began, to $379 million. The shares rose as much as 6.6% in after-hours trading and were up 2.5% around 5:23 p.m. Eastern.

How did Everpure do against its forecast?

It beat both of the measures it guides. In August the company told investors to expect revenue of $1.325 billion to $1.335 billion and adjusted operating income of $265 million to $275 million. Revenue came in at $1.46 billion. Adjusted operating income was $345 million, $70 million above the top of its range.

Product revenue, which is the sale of storage systems, was $948 million, up 77%. Subscription services revenue was $512 million, up 19%. Annual recurring revenue from subscriptions reached $2.2 billion, up 20%. Remaining performance obligations, the value of contracts not yet counted as revenue, were $4.2 billion, up 44%.

Net income was $100.4 million, or 29 cents a share, against $54.8 million, or 16 cents, a year earlier.

Growth has been speeding up for more than two years. In August Everpure said its revenue growth had accelerated for eight quarters in a row. The latest quarter makes nine. The last five readings are 16%, 20%, 35%, 38% and now 51%.

The company tied part of that to AI. It said it has won a design contract with a second of the five largest hyperscale cloud companies, and that its FlashBlade//EXA system ranked first on every checkpointing and cache measure submitted in MLPerf Storage v3.0, an industry benchmark built around AI workloads. Everpure joined the S&P 500 in September.

What does the new forecast imply?

For the current quarter, which ends around the end of January, Everpure expects revenue of $1.50 billion to $1.52 billion and adjusted operating income of $350 million to $360 million. For the full fiscal year it now expects revenue of $5.20 billion to $5.21 billion, up from $5.03 billion to $5.07 billion, and adjusted operating income of $1.08 billion to $1.09 billion, up from $940 million to $960 million.

The midpoint of the revenue forecast rose by $155 million. The quarter just reported beat the midpoint of its own forecast by $130 million. So 84% of the raise is money that has already come in.

The rest is the change to the quarter ahead. The old full-year forecast left about $1.48 billion for the fourth quarter, on TECHi's arithmetic. The new midpoint is $1.51 billion, about 2% higher.

That forecast also implies a slowdown. Revenue of $1.51 billion would be 3.4% more than the quarter just reported, which was itself 23% more than the one before. Measured against a year earlier it is growth of 42% to 43%, down from 51%. If that is what happens, it ends the run of acceleration.

Everpure's recent record suggests the range is cautious. To keep growth above 51%, it would need fourth-quarter revenue of about $1.60 billion, which is $83 million above the top of the new range. It beat the top of its range by $125 million this quarter and by $81 million in the quarter before.

Chief financial officer Tarek Robbiati said in the release that the company is also standing by a preliminary outlook for the fiscal year after this one. The release does not give those figures.

Where is the cash going?

Into components. Everpure builds its systems around flash memory. The company said in its quarterly report in September that components had become scarce and more costly, and that it raised its own prices in the first half of the fiscal year in response.

The cost shows in the margin. Gross margin was 68.0%, down from 72.3% a year earlier. On product sales alone it was 66.7%, against 71.6%, TECHi's calculation from the income statement shows. The cost of product revenue more than doubled while product revenue rose 77%.

The trend within the year is better. Product gross margin was 64.5% in the first quarter and 65.3% in the second before reaching 66.7%, which suggests the price increases are catching up with costs.

The larger effect is on the balance sheet. Inventory was $379.5 million on November 1. Three months earlier it was $106.3 million, and at the start of the fiscal year it was $75.9 million. Building it took $272 million of cash in the quarter.

A second line has grown as well. Prepaid expenses and other current assets stood at $967 million, against $356 million when the year began. The release does not break that down. In the September report most of the equivalent balance, $904 million of $1.03 billion, was money owed mainly by Everpure's contract manufacturers for components that Everpure bought itself and sold on to them, together with tax-related receivables. In other words the company has been buying parts itself and passing them to the manufacturers that assemble its systems.

Inventory and that line together come to $1.35 billion, $915 million more than at the start of the year. Part of that is unpaid bills, as accounts payable rose by $325 million. Cash and marketable securities fell to $1.14 billion from $1.55 billion.

Free cash flow recovered in the quarter, to $265 million from an outflow of $238 million in the one before. Over nine months it is $139 million, against $414 million in the same period last year, while revenue rose 42%. Capital spending in the quarter was $178 million, close to three times the level of a year earlier.

Everpure is not alone in committing cash to secure parts. Nvidia's supply commitments have reached $390 billion, most of it for memory, as TECHi reported earlier on Wednesday.

How did the stock react?

Unevenly. Everpure closed at $101.00 on Wednesday, down 0.8%, before the results. In after-hours trading it rose as high as $107.70 at 4:12 p.m. Eastern, a gain of 6.6%, according to Nasdaq's minute-by-minute data. Around 5:23 p.m. it was near $103.53, up 2.5%. After-hours trading is thin, and the company's call with analysts began at 5 p.m. Eastern. This report does not include it.

The stock's history after results is a warning against reading much into the first move. Everpure fell the day after each of its last four reports, by 27.3% last December, 10.3% in February, 14.8% in May and 8.9% in August, Nasdaq prices show. Each of those releases also said results had exceeded the top of the company's guidance.

The shares are still up 51% this year. They are 36% below their closing high of $156.97, set on October 13. At Wednesday's close the company was worth about $35 billion on its diluted share count. That is 6.8 times the revenue it forecasts for this fiscal year and about 33 times its forecast adjusted operating income.

There is a case on each side. Growth has accelerated for nine quarters, recurring revenue is $2.2 billion, and two of the largest cloud companies have chosen its technology. Against that, margins are lower than a year ago, cash is tied up in parts, and the forecast points to slower growth.

What to watch

Everpure's quarterly report, due in the coming weeks, will show what is inside its inventory and receivables. The fourth quarter will show whether revenue lands near the $1.51 billion it forecast or the $1.60 billion that would keep growth accelerating. Component prices will decide how much of that revenue it keeps as margin. TECHi's Everpure quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Keysight misses a $2 billion quarter by $6 million, then forecasts one; orders hit $2.34B
data.description:
Keysight Technologies reported revenue of $1.994 billion for the three months to October 31, 2026, up 41% from a year earlier and above the top of its own forecast, according to results released after the market closed on Thursday, November 19. That is $6 million short of the company's first $2 billion quarter. It forecast one for the quarter now under way, with revenue of $2.04 billion to $2.06 billion.

The orders say more than the revenue. Keysight took $2.34 billion of orders in the quarter, the third in a row above $2 billion, and over its fiscal year orders ran $969 million ahead of revenue, TECHi's calculation from the company's filings shows. The forecast still points to slower growth, about 28% at its midpoint after 41%. The stock was down 0.1% at $281.27 at 9:49 a.m. Eastern on Friday, shortly after the market opened.

How did Keysight do against its forecast?

It beat it, as it has every quarter for a year and a half. Keysight makes the test and measurement equipment that engineers use to design and check electronics, and much of its recent growth has come from the networking gear inside AI data centers.

In August the company told investors to expect revenue of $1.93 billion to $1.95 billion and adjusted earnings of $3.34 to $3.40 a share. Revenue came in $44 million above the top of that range. Adjusted earnings were $3.61 a share, 21 cents above the top and 89% more than a year earlier. Net income was $486 million, or $2.82 a share.

In each of the last six quarters revenue has landed above the top of the company's range. The average margin over the six is $42 million. One of them, the April quarter, looks smaller than it was: revenue that quarter was reduced by $40 million that Keysight set aside to refund tariff surcharges to customers.

Cash followed. Operations generated $507 million in the quarter and free cash flow was $465 million, 23% of revenue. Keysight ended the year with $2.92 billion of cash.

For the full fiscal year revenue was $7.16 billion, up 33%. Adjusted earnings were $11.72 a share, up 64%, and free cash flow was $1.75 billion.

Why do the orders matter?

Orders are what customers have committed to buy. Revenue is what has been delivered and billed. When orders run ahead of revenue, work is piling up to be delivered later.

That has been the pattern all year. Orders in the October quarter were $2.34 billion, 53% more than a year earlier and 12% more than in the July quarter. They were 1.17 times the quarter's revenue.

Orders exceeded revenue in each of the four quarters of the fiscal year, by $45 million, $334 million, $245 million and $345 million. That adds up to $969 million. Full-year orders were $8.13 billion, up 49%, against revenue growth of 33%.

It was not so a year and a half ago. In the July 2025 quarter orders of $1.34 billion were slightly below revenue of $1.35 billion.

Two cautions apply. Orders can be delayed or cancelled, and the release does not give a backlog figure. Part of the growth was also bought. Keysight completed three acquisitions in October 2025, the largest of them the network-testing company Spirent, and its quarterly report for July said acquisitions added five points to order growth and six to revenue growth in that quarter.

Where is the growth coming from?

From communications, and within that from AI networking. The Communications Solutions Group reported revenue of $1.50 billion, up 51% and three-quarters of the company's total. Its commercial communications business grew 73%. Its aerospace, defense and government business grew 7%.

The smaller Electronic Industrial Solutions Group, which serves chipmakers, carmakers and general electronics, reported revenue of $498 million, up 16%.

Keysight's July report said the commercial growth came from customers developing faster data center links, at speeds of 400, 800 and 1,600 gigabits a second, and from makers of optical transceivers adding factory capacity to meet demand for AI. One of those makers, Coherent, spent $775.5 million on capital projects in a single quarter, as TECHi reported on Thursday.

What does the new forecast imply?

A first $2 billion quarter, and slower growth. For the three months to the end of January, Keysight expects revenue of $2.04 billion to $2.06 billion and adjusted earnings of $3.63 to $3.69 a share.

The midpoint, $2.05 billion, is 28.1% above the same quarter a year earlier and 2.8% above the quarter just reported. Growth in the October quarter was 40.5%. Part of the difference is the acquisitions. They closed in mid-October 2025, so from this quarter they are in both years' figures and no longer lift the comparison.

The company's record suggests the range is cautious. A year ago it forecast $1.53 billion to $1.55 billion for the same quarter and reported $1.60 billion. If revenue came in above the top by the six-quarter average of $42 million, it would be about $2.10 billion, growth of 31%. That would still be slower than the quarter just ended.

The earnings forecast is flatter. Its midpoint of $3.66 a share is 69% above a year earlier and 1.4% above the $3.61 just reported.

There is also a change at the top of the finance team. Chief financial officer Neil Dougherty steps down on December 18 and will be succeeded by Jason Kary, who runs the industrial group, the company said in a filing this month. These are the last results due before the handover.

How did the stock react?

Keysight closed at $281.42 on Thursday, down 1.7%, before the results came out. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25% the same day. On Friday the shares were at $281.27 at 9:49 a.m. Eastern, shortly after the open, down 0.1% from Thursday's close.

The first move after Keysight's results has not been a reliable guide. On the day after each of its last six reports the stock fell four times and rose twice: down 0.2%, down 3.0%, up 10.0%, up 23.1%, down 0.6% and down 6.3%. The 6.3% fall came in August, after a quarter with record orders and the largest beat of the six.

At Thursday's close the shares were up 38.5% this year and 27.5% below their closing high of $388.03, set on October 6. The company was worth about $47.9 billion, 24 times its adjusted earnings for the fiscal year. It had $983 million left at the end of July under a $1.5 billion share buyback program approved a year ago.

There is a case on each side. Orders are running well ahead of revenue, the company has beaten its own forecast in each of the last six quarters, and it converts about a quarter of its revenue into free cash flow. Against that, growth is set to slow as last year's acquisitions drop out of the comparison, AI stocks have fallen sharply this month, and a new finance chief takes over in four weeks.

What to watch

Friday's close, set against the pattern of the last six reports. The annual report, due in mid-December. The handover to a new finance chief on December 18. Results for the January quarter, expected in late February, will show whether revenue clears $2.06 billion and whether orders stay above $2 billion. TECHi's Keysight quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Nvidia falls below Alphabet in market value; a $1 trillion lead is gone in two weeks
data.description:
Nvidia is worth less than Alphabet. At 11:45 a.m. Eastern on Friday, November 20, 2026, Nvidia shares were at $135.82, down 7.0% on the day, Nasdaq data show. On the 24.1 billion shares the company has outstanding, that is a market value of $3.27 trillion. Alphabet, whose shares were up 0.8%, was worth $3.37 trillion on the share counts in its latest quarterly report.

Two weeks ago the gap ran the other way, and it was $1.00 trillion wide. TECHi's calculation shows Nvidia has lost $1.22 trillion of market value since its close on November 6, falling in nine of ten sessions counting Friday's reading. Microsoft passed it on Monday, and Alphabet has now done the same.

How do Nvidia and Alphabet compare now?

Alphabet is ahead by about $97 billion. At Thursday's close Nvidia still led by $175 billion. On November 6 it led by $1.00 trillion.

The comparison uses each company's own share count. Nvidia's comes from a filing made for one of its officers on Thursday, which states 24.1 billion shares outstanding. Alphabet's quarterly report lists 5,888 million Class A shares, 827 million Class B shares and 5,579 million Class C shares as of October 21. The Class B shares do not trade, and TECHi valued them at the Class A price. Share counts move with buybacks and stock awards, so the totals are approximate.

The two companies got here differently. Alphabet's value is 3.6% lower than it was two weeks ago. Nvidia's is 27.2% lower. On Friday they moved in opposite directions.

For Nvidia to draw level at Alphabet's current value, its shares would have to trade at about $139.83. That is 3.0% above Friday's reading and still below Thursday's close of $145.98.

Apple is the largest of the four at $5.03 trillion, followed by Microsoft at $3.64 trillion. Nvidia was ahead of both Microsoft and Alphabet a week ago.

How much has Nvidia lost?

More than a quarter of its value in two weeks. Nvidia closed at $186.64 on Friday, November 6. At that price the company was worth $4.50 trillion. At Friday's reading it is worth $3.27 trillion.

This week alone accounts for $651 billion of the loss. The stock closed last Friday at $162.85 and is 16.6% below that. Friday's fall on its own is worth about $245 billion.

Measured from the top the numbers are larger. Nvidia's highest close was $239.24 on October 6, when the company was worth $5.77 trillion. It has lost 43.2% since, or $2.49 trillion.

Friday's reading is below every close since May 30, 2025, when the stock ended at $135.13.

Which days did the damage?

The first two sessions and this week. The count starts at the close on November 6, the last before Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation over that weekend. The stock was not at a high then. It was already 22.0% below its October peak, and it had dropped 9.3% on November 5 alone, a fall worth $447 billion and larger than any single day since.

On Monday, November 9, the stock fell 4.3%, and the next day it fell 5.5%. Those two sessions took $428 billion off the company's value before any announcement about its leadership. That fall on November 10, worth $236 billion, was the largest of the two weeks until Friday, when the loss at the reading was about $245 billion.

The stock recovered 2.9% on November 11. That is the only rise in the ten sessions. On November 12, the day Nvidia disclosed that Jensen Huang had resigned as chief executive, it fell 4.3%.

It has fallen every session since. The six declines through Thursday were of 4.3%, 2.0%, 4.1%, 0.4%, 2.9% and 3.3%. Friday's would be the seventh.

Has Nvidia fallen this fast before?

Not in the closing prices TECHi checked, which go back to August 2024. If Friday's reading holds, the 27.2% fall would be the largest over any ten sessions in that period. Before this month the largest was 21.1%, in the ten sessions to March 6, 2025.

What happened in those two weeks?

A run of events, most of them about how the company is run and where its chips go. TECHi has not established how much of the fall each one explains.

On November 10 the board's independent members said they had hired Joon H. Kim, a former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation announced two days earlier. Nvidia's releases do not say what is being investigated.

On November 12 Nvidia said Huang had resigned and that its finance chief, Colette Kress, would lead the company in the interim. On November 17 the board set up a committee to oversee export controls, as TECHi reported. The board has since said it does not intend to reinstate him.

Also on November 17 the company reported quarterly revenue of $115.84 billion and forecast $130.0 billion for the current quarter. The stock fell 2.9% the next day. The Wall Street Journal reported on November 17 that the Securities and Exchange Commission is examining whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors.

On November 19 a US rule limiting exports of advanced AI chips took effect. Nvidia had already stopped selling its H200 chips to China, Kress said on the earnings call, according to TechCrunch. The House Foreign Affairs Committee released license records showing how many chips Washington had approved for Chinese buyers, as TECHi reported on Friday. Late that afternoon a filing showed Nvidia's general counsel giving notice of a share sale under a plan adopted in May, as TECHi also reported.

Has the business got worse?

Not on the figures Nvidia has published. Revenue last quarter was $115.84 billion and the forecast for this one is higher. Kress told analysts that demand far exceeds supply, CBS News reported.

What has changed is the price investors put on that business. At its November 6 close Nvidia was valued at 9.7 times last quarter's revenue multiplied by four. At Friday's reading the figure is 7.1 times.

That is a statement about confidence and not about sales. The questions hanging over the company are who will run it, what the board's investigation and Congress will find, and how much of its business depends on customers that export rules now restrict. None of those has an answer yet.

Is it only Nvidia?

No. The fall has spread across the companies that build and supply AI data centers.

The ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks each morning were down 10.3% on average at about the same time on Friday, with all ten lower. They were down 4.8% before the open, as TECHi's pre-market report showed, so the day has so far been worse than the morning. The largest falls were at Micron (12.6%), AMD (11.3%) and Arista Networks (11.2%). For the week the group is down 18.5%.

The largest buyers of AI hardware have fallen less. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta were down 1.7% on average on Friday and are down 7.5% for the week. Alphabet's move past Nvidia is the clearest sign of that gap between the companies spending on AI and the companies they buy from.

What to watch

Friday's close. Nvidia would need to finish near $139.83 to end the day level with Alphabet at its current value, and any close below Thursday's $145.98 would be its seventh decline in a row. Huang is due to give a transcribed interview to three House committees on December 1, the Foreign Affairs Committee has said. Nvidia's quarterly report is due by December 4. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and Alphabet carry live prices.

data.title: US chip rule takes effect as Nvidia halts H200 sales to China, $2.4B last quarter
data.description:
The US Commerce Department's new limits on advanced AI chips take effect on Thursday, November 19, 2026, the day the rule is published in the Federal Register. Nvidia has already gone further than the rule asks. The company has stopped selling its H200 chips to China, interim chief executive Colette Kress said on its earnings call on Tuesday, according to TechCrunch. Semafor also reported the halt.

Nvidia's own filing shows what that business was worth. Shipments of that generation of data center chip to China were $2.4 billion last quarter, its results commentary says. That is 2.1% of revenue, and it equals about a fifth of what Nvidia books from customers based in China. The forecast Nvidia gave on Tuesday already assumed none of it, which changes how that forecast reads. Take the disclosed China shipments out of last quarter and the outlook implies revenue per week rising 6.4%, where the headline comparison gives 4.2%, TECHi's calculation shows.

What takes effect on Thursday?

The rule is called Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors. The Commerce Department filed it on Monday, November 16, and it runs to 117 pages. It takes effect on publication.

It does two things. It requires a US license to export, re-export or transfer advanced AI chips to five countries: Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil. Washington's stated concern is that chips sent there can be passed on to China. TECHi reported on Tuesday that customers based in those countries account for 1.3% of Nvidia's revenue at most.

The second part reaches further. The rule also covers data centers in any country that provide large amounts of computing power to companies headquartered in China and in other countries under US export controls. Data centers already serving such customers have 90 days to obtain a license. Counted from Thursday, that deadline is February 17, 2027.

China's commerce ministry has said it will take countermeasures if the rule goes ahead, as TECHi reported on Wednesday.

What did Nvidia stop?

The H200 is a data center chip from Nvidia's Hopper generation, two generations behind the Rubin systems it has just begun shipping. The White House approved its export in January, Semafor reported, and TECHi reported in August that the first deliveries were running far below what the licenses allowed.

Kress told analysts on Tuesday that Nvidia would no longer sell H200 chips to China, according to TechCrunch's account of the call, as relayed by PCMag. Semafor's account says Nvidia halted the sales as it prepared for closer scrutiny from lawmakers. Former chief executive Jensen Huang is expected to testify to Congress next month, Semafor reported. TECHi has not seen a transcript of the call.

Nvidia's written materials do not announce a halt. They contain two sentences on China. One gives the size of the shipments. The other is in the outlook: Nvidia said it is not assuming any data center computing revenue from China.

The decision follows a week in which the company's dealings with China became a governance question. Nvidia's board has set up a committee to oversee export controls, as TECHi reported on Tuesday.

How much revenue is at stake?

Start with the figure Nvidia gives. Shipments of Hopper data center products to China were $2.4 billion in the three months to October 25.

Nvidia's revenue in the quarter was $115.84 billion, so the shipments were 2.1% of the total. They were 2.2% of data center revenue, which was $107.6 billion.

Set against China alone, they matter more. A supplement filed with the results shows $11.05 billion of revenue from customers headquartered in China, including Hong Kong. The Hopper shipments equal 22% of that. Nvidia does not say how the rest is made up.

That China figure had been recovering. It was $2.97 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. Over nine months it is $23.48 billion, against $16.62 billion.

If the $2.4 billion were repeated every quarter, it would be $9.6 billion a year. One comparison gives a sense of scale. In the same quarter, every customer based outside the United States, Taiwan and China bought $1.6 billion from Nvidia between them. The halted China shipments were half as large again as that.

What does it do to the forecast?

Nothing, on Nvidia's account, because the forecast never included it. The company expects revenue of $130.0 billion this quarter, plus or minus 3%.

That makes the comparison with last quarter uneven. Last quarter's revenue had $2.4 billion of these China shipments in it. This quarter's forecast has none.

TECHi's report on the results noted that the current quarter has 14 weeks, one more than usual, and that revenue per week would rise 4.2% at the midpoint of the forecast. Remove the disclosed China shipments from last quarter and the base falls to $8.73 billion a week from $8.91 billion. The forecast is $9.29 billion a week. On that basis the increase is 6.4%.

At the bottom of Nvidia's range the increase would be 3.2%, and at the top 9.6%.

So the business outside these China sales is growing about two points faster than the headline arithmetic suggested. The halt removes revenue Nvidia had last quarter, and it does not lower what the company told investors to expect.

The larger risk is the part of the rule that covers data centers. PCMag, citing TechCrunch, reported an estimate from the investment bank Jefferies that the restrictions on remote access could cost Nvidia as much as $62 billion of data center revenue next year. Kress said on the call that demand for the Rubin chips would cover a shortfall, according to the same account. For scale, the growth target Kress gave on Tuesday implies revenue of about $741 billion next fiscal year, on TECHi's calculation. The Jefferies figure is 8% of that.

How are the five countries responding?

Carefully. Indonesia's government communications agency said in a statement to the broadcaster CNA on Wednesday that it is reviewing the measure and asking industry how it would affect operations and investment, including in data centers. It said it is open to technical talks on how the rule will apply.

Singapore's prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said the country is prepared to help the United States check how advanced chips are used there, CNA reported. Malaysia has told data centers operating in the country that they must comply with the US rules, Reuters reported.

None of the three has said it will resist. Their data center industries run on American chips.

What does it mean for Nvidia stock?

On the numbers, the H200 decision is small. It is 2% of revenue and it was already outside the forecast. Nvidia closed at $150.96 on Wednesday, its lowest close since June 2025, as TECHi reported.

The case for concern is that the rule is aimed at something harder to measure. Nvidia does not say how much of its revenue comes from data centers abroad that rent capacity to Chinese companies. Customers based outside the United States, Taiwan and China accounted for $1.6 billion last quarter, 1.4% of revenue, but a data center's customers and its owner's headquarters are not the same thing.

The case against is that Nvidia is selling everything it can make. Kress told analysts that demand still far exceeds supply, CBS News reported, and the forecast excludes China and still rises.

What to watch

The 90-day period for existing data centers ends on February 17, 2027. Nvidia's quarterly report, due by December 4, should say more about China than the results release did. Huang's expected appearance before Congress next month will keep the company's past sales there in view, and China has yet to say what its countermeasures will be. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: US cleared 879,868 Nvidia, AMD chips for China; 1.1M sought for Southeast Asia got none
data.description:
The US Commerce Department had approved the export of 879,868 advanced AI chips from Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies by May 11, 2026, according to license records the House Foreign Affairs Committee made public on Thursday, November 19. Exporters had applied to sell 3,444,160. None of the approved chips had shipped by the date of the records.

TECHi added up all 54 applications in the released table. A quarter of what was requested was approved. More than half, 1.89 million chips, was sent back without a decision, and 1.12 million of those were meant for sites in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. That is more than Washington approved for China itself, and those three countries are among the five that a new US chip rule covers from this week.

What did the committee release?

Two documents. One is a two-page summary written by the committee. The other is a table from the Bureau of Industry and Security, the Commerce Department agency that issues export licenses, headed with the status of applications as of May 11, 2026. It lists each application by date, exporter, buyer and number of chips.

The chips covered are Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X. The buyers are companies based in China or owned by a parent there, which is why applications for data centers in Southeast Asia appear on the list.

The committee's Republican chairman, Brian Mast, released the records under a provision of the Export Control Reform Act that lets the committee publish license information when it decides secrecy is against the national interest. The disclosure was approved by unanimous consent, the committee's senior Democrat, Gregory Meeks, said in a statement. The committee called it the most detailed disclosure of its kind under the act.

What do the numbers show?

The table sorts the applications into four groups.

Twenty-one were approved, for 879,868 chips, which is 25.5% of everything requested. Nine were marked RWA, the agency's abbreviation for returned without action, for 1,888,950 chips, or 54.8%. Twenty-three were still under review, for 600,342 chips. One was rejected: AMD's request to sell 75,000 chips to the cloud company UCloud.

Set aside the applications still pending and 30.9% of the chips with an outcome were approved.

The largest requests did not get through. Nvidia asked in February to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba, and in December to supply 508,000 to a ByteDance unit in Malaysia. Both were returned.

A ceiling is visible in the approvals. None is for more than 75,000 chips, and nine of the 21 are for exactly that number. TECHi reported in August that the licenses allow up to 75,000 chips for each approved customer.

Who was approved?

ByteDance and Tencent received the most. Each had one Nvidia application and one AMD application approved at 75,000 chips, for 150,000 apiece. Didi was approved for 99,780 across the two suppliers. Alibaba, Kuaishou, VNET and Linkwise Digital were each approved for 75,000. The game developer miHoYo was approved for 57,810, Baidu for 43,000 and JD.com for 41,300.

Carmakers are on the list in smaller numbers. Li Auto was approved for 8,260 chips, Great Wall Motor for 4,800, and BYD and Tesla's Shanghai unit for 4,000 each.

The committee's summary says four of the approved buyers are on the Pentagon's list of Chinese military companies: Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu and BYD. Their approvals total 272,000 chips, or 30.9% of the total. That list restricts Pentagon contracting. It is not an export blacklist.

The two suppliers fared differently. Nvidia had 17 applications approved for 579,868 chips, 65.9% of the approved total. AMD had four approved for 300,000. Every one of AMD's eight applications was for exactly 75,000 chips, and half of what it asked for was approved. For Nvidia the share was 20.6%, because its largest requests were the ones sent back.

Why does Southeast Asia matter?

Five of the returned applications were not for China at all. Nvidia applied in December 2025 to supply 1,118,500 chips to units of ByteDance, TikTok and Alibaba Cloud in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. That is 32.5% of everything requested, and 1.3 times what was approved for China.

None of it was approved. All five applications were returned without action.

Those are three of the five countries named in the Commerce rule that took effect on Thursday, which requires a license to send advanced AI chips there and covers data centers that serve Chinese companies. The records show the scale of the demand the rule is aimed at. They also show that the largest requests of that kind were already being turned back in the months before it was written.

Did the chips reach China?

Not by May. Every one of the 21 approvals carries the same note in the table: approved, not shipped.

Deliveries began later and stayed small. ByteDance and Tencent had each received about 10,000 H200 chips by August, the Financial Times reported, 13% of what one license allows. Nvidia's results show $2.4 billion of shipments of that generation of chip to China in the three months to October 25. The company has since stopped selling the H200 to China, its interim chief executive told analysts on Tuesday, according to accounts of the call.

So 879,868 is what was permitted. It is not what arrived, and the released documents do not say how many chips were delivered.

What are lawmakers alleging?

The committee's release says the applications include requests by Nvidia to rely on what it calls possible chip-smuggling fronts. Its summary says all but two of Nvidia's applications name four companies that might install the systems: Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies, ZTE Kangxun Telecom and Lenovo. It cites New York Times reports that raised questions about the risk of chips being diverted through two of those companies and a third. Mast said at Thursday's meeting that he believes two of them are fronts, Quartz reported, citing CNBC.

These are allegations by lawmakers. The documents make no finding against any company, and TECHi has not seen responses from the companies named. The summary also notes that every application described the risk of diversion as low. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment, according to Quartz.

Meeks said the record shows the agency approving licenses with little scrutiny while other reviews were delayed. He called for public hearings with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and the head of the bureau, Jeffrey Kessler.

What does it mean for Nvidia and AMD stock?

Both fell on Thursday, in a market that fell with them. Nvidia closed down 3.3% at $145.98 and AMD down 7.7% at $489.19, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.25%. At 5:52 a.m. Eastern on Friday, before the market opened, Nvidia was at $142.97 and AMD at $465.95.

For Nvidia the sales at stake are already out of its forecast. Those China shipments were 2.1% of revenue last quarter, and the outlook it gave on Tuesday assumes none. The records matter more as evidence in the argument over how export controls were run, which now includes hearings and proposals for new legislation.

For AMD the records give a detailed count of its licensed China business. They show approval to sell 300,000 MI325X chips. They do not show how many it sold.

What to watch

The 23 applications still pending, covering 600,342 chips, and whether any are decided now that Nvidia has stopped H200 sales. Hearings, if Lutnick and Kessler are called. Jensen Huang is due to give a transcribed interview to three House committees on December 1, and Nvidia's general counsel on December 2, the committee has said. Data centers already serving Chinese companies have until February 17, 2027 to obtain licenses under the new rule. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and AMD carry live prices.

data.title: Premarket: AI hardware stocks down 4.8%; Thursday’s 3.9% early gain ended as a 3.5% loss
data.description:
Ten AI hardware stocks were down 4.8% on average before the US market opened on Friday, November 20, 2026, according to Nasdaq pre-market quotes read at 7:20 a.m. Eastern. Nvidia was down 2.7% at $142.07. All ten were lower.

The same ten were up 3.9% at this hour on Thursday, as TECHi reported. They closed down 3.5%. Every one of them finished lower, a swing of 7.4 points between the morning reading and the close, TECHi's calculation shows. It was the second day running that an early gain did not hold, and this time the group gave back more than the whole of it.

Where do AI stocks stand before the open?

Lower across the board. The ten hardware and infrastructure names TECHi tracks each morning were down 4.8% on average at 7:20 a.m. Eastern. From weakest to strongest, AMD was down 6.0%, Dell 5.6%, CoreWeave 5.3%, Micron 5.1%, Marvell 5.1%, Vertiv 4.7%, Super Micro 4.5%, TSMC 4.5%, Arista Networks 3.9% and Broadcom 3.5%.

Nvidia, which TECHi counts separately because of its size, was at $142.07, down 2.7% from Thursday's close of $145.98.

The four largest buyers of AI hardware were down 1.5% on average. Alphabet was down 0.2%, Microsoft 1.6%, Amazon 1.9% and Meta 2.4%. As on Thursday, they were holding up better than the companies that supply them.

The ten are Broadcom, AMD, Arista Networks, Vertiv, Super Micro, TSMC, Micron, Marvell, Dell and CoreWeave. Between them they cover chip design, chip manufacturing, memory, networking, servers, power and cooling, and rented computing capacity. The average is unweighted, so CoreWeave counts for as much as Broadcom.

Pre-market prices come from thin trading and often change before the bell. The readings here are the middle value of the last five one-minute prices for each stock.

What happened to Thursday's early gain?

It turned into a loss. At 6:14 a.m. on Thursday the ten stocks were up 3.9% on average and Nvidia was up 2.1%. By the close the group was down 3.5% and Nvidia was down 3.3%.

TECHi's Thursday report set a marker: half of the early gain, about 2.0%, kept at the close. The group missed it by more than five points. All ten closed below their Wednesday close, and all ten closed below where they had traded that morning.

AMD fell most, 7.7%. CoreWeave lost 6.1%, and Vertiv and Marvell lost 4.9% each. Dell came closest to holding, down 0.2%.

Measured from the morning, the reversals were larger. CoreWeave went from a gain of 5.4% before the open to a loss of 6.1% at the close, a swing of 11.5 points. AMD went from up 3.2% to down 7.7%, and Marvell from up 4.5% to down 4.9%.

AMD has been the most volatile of the ten. It rose 5.3% on Wednesday, fell 7.7% on Thursday and was down a further 6.0% before Friday's open.

The buyers fell too. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta lost 3.1% on average, after being up 2.4% before the open. Alphabet had been up 4.1% that morning and closed down 3.5%.

It is the second morning in a row to mislead. On Wednesday the group was up 4.0% before the open and finished up 0.7%. On Thursday it was up 3.9% and finished down 3.5%. The morning reading overstated the close by 3.3 points one day and 7.4 the next.

How bad is the week?

For Nvidia, the worst part of a bad fortnight. Thursday's close of $145.98 was its lowest since June 23, 2025. The stock is down 10.4% since last Friday's close of $162.85, after falling 12.7% the week before. Over the nine sessions since November 6 it has lost 21.8%. It is 39.0% below its closing high of $239.24, set on October 6, and it has closed lower for six sessions in a row.

At $142.07 before the open, Nvidia was 12.8% below last Friday's close. A close at that level would take the loss since November 6 to 23.9%.

The hardware group stood 9.2% below last Friday's close at Thursday's close. At Friday's pre-market readings it was 13.5% below.

Within the group the week has been uneven. Through Thursday's close, CoreWeave was down 15.5% since last Friday, TSMC and Marvell 11.7% each, and Micron and Super Micro 11.3% each. Dell was down 9.3%, Vertiv 8.5% and AMD 8.4%. Two names have held: Arista Networks was down 3.9% and Broadcom 0.1%.

The buyers have lost less. Alphabet was down 7.8% for the week at Thursday's close, Meta 7.1%, Microsoft 4.9% and Amazon 3.5%.

The wider market has fallen with them. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.25% on Thursday to close at 23,879.20.

What is weighing on the stocks?

TECHi has not established a single cause, and several things arrived at once.

Anthropic's first day of trading did not lift the sector as early prices on Thursday had suggested it might. The stock opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17, keeping half of its opening gain, as TECHi reported earlier on Friday. It was lower again before Friday's open, at $87.97 at 7:20 a.m. Eastern, 9.5% below Thursday's close.

Washington is another source of pressure. Records released by a House committee on Thursday show the US approved 879,868 Nvidia and AMD chips for Chinese buyers and sent back applications for far more, as TECHi reported. Lawmakers from both parties want hearings. A new rule on chip exports took effect on Thursday, and Nvidia has stopped selling its H200 chips to China.

Nvidia itself is without a permanent chief executive. Jensen Huang is due to give a transcribed interview to three House committees on December 1.

None of that is new this morning. What is new is that two rallies in two days have failed.

Does a weak morning tell you anything?

Not much, on this week's evidence. Both of the last two mornings pointed up and both closes came in lower than the morning. That says early prices have been a poor guide to the day. It does not say which way they will be wrong.

There is a simple marker for Friday. If the ten stocks close above their pre-market level, it will be the first of the three sessions TECHi has tracked this way in which the day improved on the morning. If they close below it, the group's loss for the week will be larger than the 13.5% the early readings imply.

What else is on the calendar?

Friday is the monthly expiration date for US stock options, which can add to volume and to price swings late in the session. Next week is a short one. US markets are closed on Thursday, November 26, for Thanksgiving and close early the day after.

Two dates further out matter for the chip stocks. Nvidia's quarterly report to the Securities and Exchange Commission is due by December 4 and should say more about its China business than the results release did. Data centers that already serve Chinese customers have until February 17, 2027 to obtain licenses under the new export rule.

What to watch

The opening bell at 9:30 a.m. Eastern and whether the early losses narrow. Nvidia's close against $145.98, and whether it ends a second week down by a tenth or more. A close below $144.17 would put it under every close since June 20, 2025. AMD, the weakest of the group for two sessions. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and AMD carry live prices.

data.title: Premarket: AI hardware stocks up 3.9%; Wednesday’s 4.0% early gain ended the day at 0.7%
data.description:
Stocks tied to AI hardware rose in pre-market trading on Thursday, November 19, 2026, hours before Anthropic's shares are due to begin trading. At 6:14 a.m. Eastern the ten hardware stocks TECHi tracks were up 3.9% on average, according to Nasdaq quotes. CoreWeave and Micron led with gains of 5.4%. Nvidia was up 2.1%.

Wednesday is the reason to be careful with that number. The same ten stocks were up 4.0% before the open a day earlier, after Nvidia reported results above its own forecast, and they finished the session up 0.7%. On TECHi's calculation 83% of the early gain was gone by the close. Nvidia itself turned a 2.9% pre-market rise into a 2.9% fall.

Which AI stocks are moving?

The gains are broad. Every one of the ten hardware stocks was higher, and so were the four largest spenders on AI data centers.

CoreWeave, which rents out computing capacity built on Nvidia chips, was up 5.4% at $50.41. Micron, which makes memory chips, was up 5.4% at $743.31. Super Micro Computer, which builds AI servers, was up 4.6% at $25.48. Marvell, which designs custom and networking chips for data centers, was up 4.5% at $152.06. Dell, which builds AI servers, was up 4.3% at $326.80. Vertiv, which makes power and cooling equipment for data centers, was up 3.9% at $202.13. Arista Networks, which sells data center networking gear, was up 3.5% at $200.74. AMD, which is Nvidia's main rival in AI chips, was up 3.2% at $547.05. Broadcom, which sells custom AI chips and networking chips, was up 3.1% at $364.99. TSMC, which manufactures chips for Nvidia and others, was up 1.2% at $366.89.

Among the spenders, the moves were Alphabet 4.1%, Amazon 2.6%, Meta 1.5% and Microsoft 1.3%. Before the open on Wednesday the four were up 0.6% on average. On Thursday morning they were up 2.4%.

Alphabet has a direct interest in the day's main event. Its Google unit agreed to buy about $10.0 billion of Anthropic stock in a private sale alongside the public offering, Anthropic's prospectus says. Anthropic priced its shares at $83 on Wednesday evening, above its range, as TECHi reported overnight. Reuters reported that Nasdaq futures rose on hopes for a strong debut.

Oracle, which both buys Nvidia chips and sells cloud capacity, was up 2.6%. Shares of TSMC here are its US-listed depositary shares. Pre-market trading on Nasdaq runs from 4 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. Eastern, and volumes are a fraction of a normal session.

What happened to Wednesday's early gains?

Most of them faded. TECHi recorded the same group at 4:27 a.m. on Wednesday and published the result. The ten hardware stocks were up 4.0% on average and all ten were higher.

By the 4 p.m. close the average gain was 0.7%. Four of the ten ended the day lower: CoreWeave, Dell, Marvell and Micron. Only three finished above where they stood before the open. Those were AMD, Broadcom and Arista Networks. Four kept at least half of their early gain.

Nvidia was the clearest case. It was up 2.9% before the open and closed down 2.9%, at its lowest closing price since June 2025, as TECHi reported on Wednesday. The same report found that Nvidia has closed below its opening price on the day after nine of its last ten earnings releases.

The spenders went the other way. They were up 0.6% before Wednesday's open and ended the day up 1.2%. Amazon went from a 0.9% early gain to a 3.8% rise at the close. Alphabet held its 0.8%, Microsoft finished up 0.4%, and Meta slipped from a small gain to a loss of 0.4%.

The reversals were large. CoreWeave went from a gain of 6.7% before the open to a loss of 4.1% at the close. Dell went from 4.7% up to 2.9% down, Marvell from 3.9% up to 2.2% down, and Micron from 3.8% up to 1.0% down. TSMC and Super Micro Computer each gave back more than three points and finished about 1% higher. AMD, Broadcom and Arista Networks did the opposite and added to their early gains, with AMD ending the day up 5.3%.

Thursday's rebound is strongest where Wednesday's selling was. All four hardware stocks that closed lower on Wednesday are among the five biggest pre-market gainers.

Where does each stock stand for the week?

Still lower, for most. The group fell hard over the first three sessions of the week. From Friday's close to Wednesday's, the ten hardware stocks lost 5.8% on average. CoreWeave, Micron, Super Micro Computer, TSMC and Dell each lost about 9%.

Thursday's pre-market gains repair part of that. On average the five have recovered 40% of the three-day loss. Measured against last Friday's close, the ten hardware stocks were down 2.2% on average at Thursday's pre-market prices. The four spenders were down 0.4%.

Four of the fifteen stocks in the table were above Friday's close: Broadcom by 5.2%, Amazon by 3.0%, AMD by 2.4% and Arista Networks by 1.7%. Vertiv was level with Friday's close. TSMC was furthest below, down 8.0%.

Nvidia was 5.4% below Friday's close of $162.85. From its pre-market price of $154.09 it would need to rise another 5.7% to get back there.

Why is Nvidia lagging again?

Its 2.1% gain put it near the bottom of the group. Only TSMC had gained less. That was also the pattern on Wednesday morning, when Nvidia's rise was smaller than the average for the companies that supply it and compete with it.

Nvidia has fallen in seven of the eight sessions since November 6 and has lost 19.1% over that stretch, while AMD has gained 18.1%.

The reasons investors give have not changed. Nvidia has an interim chief executive and a board that is searching for a permanent one. A US rule limiting exports of advanced AI chips takes effect on Thursday, and Nvidia has stopped selling its H200 chips to China, as TECHi reported earlier on Thursday.

The price reflects it. At $154.09, Nvidia trades at 9.9 times the earnings analysts expect for the fiscal year that ends in January 2028, on Nasdaq's consensus of $15.55 a share.

There is a case for the other side. Nvidia's revenue was $115.8 billion last quarter and it forecast $130 billion for this one. At under ten times next year's expected earnings, the stock is priced for little of that growth.

Will the gains hold this time?

Wednesday's record says not to assume so. The early gain then was bigger, it followed results that beat forecasts, and it mostly disappeared.

A simple marker follows from that record. If the hardware group keeps half of Thursday's early gain, it will close up about 2.0%. On Wednesday it kept about a sixth.

There is one difference. Wednesday's rise was a reaction to a single company's report. Thursday's comes with a new stock arriving. Anthropic's listing is the largest on record, according to Reuters, and seven chip and cloud companies are buying $26.0 billion of its stock in the private sale. How the shares trade will be read as a verdict on demand for AI itself.

What to watch

The regular session opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern. Anthropic's first trade is expected later in the day, under the symbol ANT. The comparison to make at 4 p.m. is the one TECHi made on Wednesday: how much of the morning's gain is left. TECHi's quote pages for Nvidia and Alphabet carry live prices.
